articles.title: iPhone Duo reviews: The absolute best foldable phone, but not without compromise
articles.author: Ben Lovejoy
articles.content:
We posted our own review of the iPhone Duo yesterday, and Chance Miller was left convinced that “this form factor represents the future of the iPhone,” while acknowledging that the first-gen iPhone Duo comes with trade-offs.
I think what surprised me most is the degree of consensus found across the reviews, given the generally polarized appeal of foldable phones. That’s not to say reviewers think everyone should buy one, but there is widespread agreement on the pros and cons – starting with five key takeouts …
Five key takeouts
First, all the reviews I’ve read and watched say that the iPhone Duo is hands-down the best foldable phone on the market. Apple waited a very long time before joining the foldable party, and it seems clear that it was absolutely right to do so.
Second, this phone is absolutely not for everyone. Even leaving aside the high purchase cost, the form factor currently involves compromises that would rule it out for some. If you expect to use the outer screen most of the time and only unfold it a few times a day, then the trade-offs of the heavy weight when held in one hand and the unusual display shape are just too big a drawback. This phone really only makes sense if you expect to make frequent use of the larger unfolded screen in your day-to-day use.
Third, Apple hasn’t made the crease invisible, and indeed has made no claims to do so. You can see it in certain lights at certain angles, and you can feel it when running your finger across the screen. But everyone agrees that this is the least intrusive crease ever seen on a foldable, and that it’s simply not an issue in real life use. More on this in a moment.
Fourth, a great many apps haven’t yet been updated, and in the worst case that means seeing an iPhone screen layout stranded in the middle of a mostly black inner display. The optimistic view is that this will rapidly change, but be prepared for some disappointments with third-party apps in early usage.
Finally, going back to Touch ID is a significant compromise after being used to Face ID. We do have to bear in mind that reviewers have only had a chance to use the device for a week, but certainly in that time most say they didn’t really get used to it and would absolutely prefer Face ID.
Fold testing
A couple of reviewers used machines to subject the iPhone Duo to thousands of folds and unfolds to test two things. Does the crease become significantly more visible over time, and how does the hinge hold up?
In both cases, there is a measurable impact. Joanna Stern’s tests found that the hinge is affected across tens of thousands of folds, but interestingly becomes stiffer rather than looser – the opposite of what we would expect. However, while this change was measurable using a strain gauge after 32,000 folds, she said she couldn’t feel it in normal use.
HTX Studio did the most scientific testing of the impact of thousands of folds on the crease. The depth of the crease when new was measured at just 48 microns, about half the thickness of a sheet of paper, while the slope of the crease measured at less than 0.1 degrees – both markedly better than competing foldables. After 3,000 folds, the depth of the crease increased to 167 microns and the slope increased to 1.24 degrees. That brings it more in line with the measurements of other foldables after the same number of tests.
The bottom line
There are links to the full reviews, but here is the bottom line from each …
After 20 years of iPhones that look mostly the same, it’s exciting to see Apple chart a new course. But the Duo is still one of the most early adopter Apple products I’ve tested in a long time. It’s easy to imagine what Gen 2 will look like. It’s lighter, there’s Face ID, a better camera inside, and hopefully a lower price. Also, it’s got a telephoto camera, and it’s no longer a hand warmer.
The good news is most of my other frustrations can be fixed with software updates and developers figuring out how to make great apps for two very different screen sizes. Sure, early adopters have to navigate some choppy waters, but as Apple developers catch up, I can see smoother sailing ahead.
Apple’s first attempt [at a foldable] brings plenty of fresh ideas with real purpose behind them that deserves credit. But think about it: these ideas mostly fix flaws built into the folding design rather than pushing the phone experience forward.
[Will this make foldables mainstream?] I still doubt it because this design has two fundamental conflicts at its core. First, the [aspect ratios] of two screens work against each other. Improve the outer screen and the inner screen becomes a big empty square. Favor the inner screen [as Apple has done] and the outer screen becomes a passport that’s hard to grip. It’s a zero-sum game. More importantly, whatever the balance, you get a makeshift phone outside and a cut down tablet inside. Neither delivers the best
experience.
Second, the benefits are occasional, but the cost are constant. To fit a hinge and the big screen, it sacrifices weight, battery life, cooling, performance, cameras, and most importantly, price. But use one or watch other people do and you’ll see they mostly use the outer screen […] You enjoy the benefits some of the time but pay the price all the time.
If you really want to do something, or sit back and read or watch something, the big display is fantastic. But that Duo-as-tablet experience is so cumbersome compared to the “just look at it” experience of using a regular iPhone uno that you simply cannot do it every time you use the Duo. You will use the outer display quite a bit. And using the outer display delivers the worst iPhone experience ever. I mean, some iPhone has to be the one that offered the worst iPhone experience ever. That iPhone is the outer half of the iPhone Duo […]
If you’d rather trade your iPhone for an iPad Mini that you can fold in half to carry around, the iPhone Duo might be the form factor for you. Even if that’s the case, though, this first iPhone Duo might not suit you, for all the various irritations and shortcomings I’ve documented […] It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry.
CNET:
Aside from some minor shortcomings, Apple appears to have stuck the landing with its long-awaited foldable. Hopefully, future iterations will add elements such as Face ID while improving the camera capabilities, either by adding a telephoto lens or bolstering the inner screen’s FaceTime camera. It would be nice to see multitasking become more dynamic in the future, too.
[But] most people just don’t need a phone that doubles as a tablet. [While the Duo] is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general, I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.
Whether you’re an iPhone fan, foldable evangelist, or Android user who’s just been waiting to see what Apple offers, I think we can all agree that the iPhone Duo has already achieved what competing foldables have not been able to in seven years: generate considerable buzz for foldable phones […] This is what we’ve been waiting for after more than a decade of matured bar-style phones. Finally, phone hardware and software are genuinely exciting again, which is something to celebrate […]
As for whether you should get the iPhone Duo—that depends on if you can afford it, either buying it outright, paying in installments, or leasing it through the Apple Upgrade program. Do you want a foldable phone, and why? Will you use the larger screen often, and how much value will you get from it? Will the weight bother you? Do you need better cameras? There are so many personal factors to consider before you decide. The iPhone Duo isn’t the “definitive” iPhone to own. Apple’s iPhone lineup now caters to every budget and every type of user. Only you can be honest with yourself about your needs.
Top comment by sean roberts
The absolute best foldable? Not sure which videos you watch but from what I can see, the phone is too heavy and needs the software to catch up. If this was a Android phone, you guys would be calling it the worst phone ever that nobody will buy. It has potential but I suspect a lot of the pre orders will be returned by customers who expect it to work great straight away. Not every buyer will want to wait for the devs to catch up, which they will but it will take some time.
The iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable phone I’ve ever tested, with a sturdy and premium build and a nano-texture display that hides the crease. I also like the multiple usage modes and split-screen multitasking. However, while fully updated apps for the Duo look great, non-optimized apps do not. And the lack of a telephoto zoom is a bummer for a $2,000 phone […]
I like the iPhone Duo’s nano texture display in that it greatly reduces glare outdoors and minimizes the crease better than any foldable I’ve tested. But you give up perfect blacks with this matte panel and more saturated colors versus the iPhone 18 Pro Max. You also sacrifice a telephoto lens and Face ID. I can live with those trade-offs, but that doesn’t mean I like them.
In a way it’s a good thing that the iPhone Duo is backordered for many until December or January. That will give developers plenty of time to update their offerings for this foldable. I don’t think it will take that long, though, based on the high demand.
Overall, though, I think the iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable yet with the most polished, intuitive and fun software experience.
This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues but because I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.
Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but, on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).
But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.
There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way. It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief […] But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going […]
We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time […] Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera […]
But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time […] The real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.
What’s your take after reading the review conclusions? Have the reviews made you more or less interested in the iPhone Duo? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

articles.title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
Governments and some of the world's biggest companies are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws.
The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them.
A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement., external
Amazon said its threat intelligence system identified it was targeted on Saturday. It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted.
The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability."
PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web.
Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites.
As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like."
"They can steal data , they can go to other parts of your network. All sort of things like that - even plant a backdoor to get in later on, so it's pretty serious," Woodward told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language.
He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI".
Austin described PHP as "one of the first web languages that powered the early internet".
"It's in a lot of places that you wouldn't expect to be that are basically very core to how the internet runs in a lot of ways. It's like all the old things that are in a house that you know keeps it [running] but you don't really think about," the PHP researcher said.
But Austin said this incident is not necessarily bad news because organisations would now "run and patch PHP immediately" if they haven't already.
Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October.
In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said.
The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said.
While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.
In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said.
The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning.
The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added.
The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days".
She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said.
The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade.
Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure.
The websites for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors are currently inaccessible.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it had followed guidance to take its website offline, "in view of the critical security issues affecting PHP".
Edinburgh and Oxford council websites also went offline on Wednesday, but are now accessible.
The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website.
This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed.
The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database".
It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update.
OpenAI called the discovery, "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
articles.summary:
The UK government and global organizations are rushing to patch critical security flaws in the PHP programming language that potentially expose millions of websites to malicious cyberattacks.

### Key Points
- Researcher Ryan Austin discovered the critical PHP vulnerability, which had remained undetected for at least a decade.
- The flaw allows attackers to execute unauthorized code, steal sensitive data, or plant backdoors on affected web servers.
- Amazon reported detecting and blocking multiple "PHP2Shell" exploitation attempts targeting its systems following a premature leak of the vulnerability details.
- Government agencies in the UK, EU, Australia, and Finland have advised organizations to apply patches immediately or take vulnerable systems offline.
- Estimates suggest the vulnerability impacts a significant portion of the internet, including major platforms like Wikipedia and WordPress.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing role of artificial intelligence in both discovering complex software vulnerabilities and enabling attackers to exploit them rapidly. Because PHP underpins a vast segment of the global web infrastructure, these flaws pose a systemic risk to data security and service availability for both public and private sectors.

articles.title: Google’s Illyes: Robots.txt Covers Crawling, Not AI Training via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.author: Matt G. Southern
articles.content:
Robots.txt, as the internet standard RFC 9309 defines it, governs which URLs a crawler may request, not what happens to the content afterward, Google’s Gary Illyes said in a Search Central video published Wednesday. To keep one AI crawler out while allowing others, he said, you have to target that crawler’s user-agent token in the file.
The video is the second episode of The Non-Canonical Cabinet, where Illyes and Cherry Prommawin of Google Search Relations take edge-case questions from the community. Illyes is also co-author, with Mozilla’s Martin Thomson, of an IETF Internet-Draft that would give robots.txt a standard way to state usage preferences. Prommawin recommended writing non-English rule paths in percent-encoded form for crawlers other than Google’s.
What Illyes Said About AI Training
The episode’s question was whether robots.txt can allow AI crawling of a website and keep that same information out of generative model training. According to Illyes, “So as defined by RFC 9309, robots.txt is an access preference protocol.” He went on to say robots.txt “doesn’t dictate what a system does with the data after it has already crawled it.” If you want to completely block a specific AI crawler from accessing your entire website, Illyes stated, you need to “target their specific user agent tokens explicitly in the file.”
The episode illustrated a fictional directive (e.g., No-AI-Chicken-Training) which was shown on-screen and would be ignored by a parser. Google’s robots.txt specification page states that the four elements supported are User-Agent, Allow, Disallow, and Sitemap; invalid lines will be ignored by Google.
As for RFC 9309 specifically (Section 2.2.4), it allows crawlers to decide how they’ll process a record outside the scope of this protocol. Therefore, whether or not an additional line accomplishes something depends on the crawler interpreting it.
What Google-Extended Controls
Google-Extended is a robots.txt token with no user agent of its own. Google crawls under its existing user agents, and Google’s list of common crawlers says the token is “used in a control capacity.” It manages whether content Google crawls can be used to train future Gemini models and for grounding in Gemini Apps and Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI. The page says it doesn’t affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search and isn’t a ranking signal.
Google-Extended’s meaning as a usage control comes from Google’s documentation for its own products, rather than RFC 9309. The hosts didn’t discuss it on air, but the video’s description links to the same list.
The Draft That Would Add A Usage Rule
The current version of the IETF draft Illyes co-wrote, dated Aug. 19, would update RFC 9309, if approved, with a Content-Usage rule for robots.txt and a matching HTTP header. Neither the episode nor its description mentions the draft.
Under the draft, Allow and Disallow would continue to govern which URLs can be crawled. Content-Usage would then define preferences as to how crawled content should be used. Those preferences would only relate to paths where a crawler has permission to fetch content. A Content-Usage field of “train-ai=n” is added to the draft’s example robots.txt file, which allows crawling.
The draft is still a Working Group Document. At present, its IETF Datatracker entry shows that the Working Group has not yet submitted the document for review by the IETF’s Steering Group (IESG). The Working Group’s planned date for sending it to the IESG was Aug. 2026. The ‘train-ai’ Label referenced above appears in a separate Vocabulary Draft, dated Sept. 14. That document states that it reflects no consensus within the Working Group.
Percent-Encode Non-English Paths
Cherry Prommawin’s advice for paths with non-English characters or emoji was that “you should use the encoded version in your robots.txt rules.” Google’s parser handles raw characters by encoding them, she said, but “other or older crawlers on the web might get confused.”
The on-screen example labeled a raw emoji path “Works for Google, might break others” and its percent-encoded form “The Safe, Standard Way.” Google’s spec page says its parser treats raw UTF-8 and percent-encoded paths the same way, and RFC 9309’s grammar allows UTF-8 characters in paths.
Why This Matters
The method you would need in robots.txt to limit AI use of your content while keeping your site visible in Google Search depends on what bot or product you are working with. Disallow statements may prevent specific AI crawlers from accessing particular webpages. For Gemini, the documented control of Google is Google-Extended and includes both training and grounding. There currently is no standard way of expressing a training preference independent of the bots allowed to crawl the webpage; one exists only as a draft.
Websites that use URLs with languages other than English will want to encode their robots.txt paths using percent encoding. Percent encoding is safer because, although Google treats both raw and encoded versions of the same robots.txt rule path equally, other crawlers could potentially interpret raw characters differently.
Looking Ahead
According to the video description, the next Non-Canonical Cabinet episode will cover the 404 status code. The current Content-Usage draft is set to expire on Feb. 20, 2027, unless a new revision replaces it sooner.

articles.summary:
Google’s Gary Illyes clarified that the robots.txt protocol only governs URL access and cannot restrict how AI models use data once it has been successfully crawled.

### Key Points
- The RFC 9309 standard defines robots.txt as an access preference protocol, not a tool for controlling post-crawl data usage by AI systems.
- To block specific AI crawlers, website owners must explicitly target the crawler’s unique user-agent token within their robots.txt file.
- Google-Extended is a specific token used to manage whether Google crawls content for training Gemini models or for grounding in Vertex AI.
- An IETF Internet-Draft co-authored by Illyes proposes a new "Content-Usage" rule, though it is not yet an official standard and lacks industry consensus.
- Cherry Prommawin recommends using percent-encoded paths for non-English characters in robots.txt to ensure compatibility with older or non-Google web crawlers.

### Why it Matters
Website owners currently lack a universal standard to prevent AI training while still allowing search engine indexing, forcing them to rely on specific bot-by-bot exclusions. This technical limitation highlights the growing gap between existing web protocols and the complex data-usage requirements of modern generative artificial intelligence.

articles.title: ‘VPNs at Risk’: Tech Coalition Pushes Back on Piracy Blocking Duties for VPNs
articles.author: Ernesto Van der Sar
articles.content:
When Rep. Darrell Issa introduced his site blocking bill last month, VPN providers made the list.
The American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA) would allow courts to order ISPs, DNS resolvers, and VPNs to block foreign pirate sites.
The competing DEFEND IP Act, introduced days later by Rep. Zoe Lofgren and Sen. Thom Tillis, does the opposite. It explicitly excludes services that only offer VPNs.
The VPN industry has a voice in U.S. blocking debates through the Internet Infrastructure Coalition (i2Coalition). In addition to representing companies such as Amazon, Cloudflare, and Google, the group runs a VPN Trust Initiative, with ExpressVPN, NordVPN, and Surfshark as founding members.
The coalition has been relatively quiet in recent site blocking discussions, but today, on Global Encryption Day, i2Coalition published a report titled “VPNs at Risk.”
Like last year’s DNS at Risk report, it warns against turning neutral infrastructure into a copyright enforcement tool.
From Pirate Sites to VPNs
Copyright enforcement is one of the reasons governments consider regulating VPNs, the report notes. VPNs can be used to bypass blocking measures and may make it harder for rightsholders to identify infringers or enforce geographic licensing restrictions.
France has been one of the prime examples of this type of regulation, i2Coalition notes. In May 2025, a Paris court ordered NordVPN, CyberGhost, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Proton VPN to block 203 pirate sports streaming domains at the request of Canal+.
“These cases, brought by rightsholders before French courts, illustrate how obligations imposed at one layer of the Internet can migrate to another when users find alternative technical paths around court-ordered restrictions,” the report notes.
That raises a broader question.
According to the report, the issue is not just which intermediaries can be ordered to block, but whether these measures actually reduce piracy, and what side effects they have for lawful users.
The French legal battle isn’t over either.
The report describes the decisions as “currently pending appeal,” but it doesn’t mention the latest twists. On September 30, the Paris Court of Appeal put an appeal by NordVPN, Proton, and CyberGhost against a similar order, obtained by football league LFP, on hold. It will first wait for a ruling from France’s Supreme Court, the Cour de cassation, in related DNS blocking cases.
A week later, the Paris court refused beIN’s request for daily penalties against VPN providers and Cloudflare, which had not fully blocked the targeted sites.
i2Coalition is aware of these developments but will keep the report text as is.
“We’re following those proceedings, including the pending Cour de cassation outcome. We’re keeping the text for this release, but those developments will inform future updates. They don’t change our broader concern about the implications of extending blocking obligations to VPN providers,” Executive Director Christian Dawson tells us.
Target the Right Layer
The report doesn’t ask for a VPN exemption from any and all regulation. Instead, it urges lawmakers to be precise, and to take measures where they make the most sense.
“Policymakers should consider where meaningful knowledge and control actually reside and whether an obligation can be directed toward the relevant conduct or service before moving deeper into general-purpose Internet infrastructure. The further an intervention moves from the activity being regulated, the greater the need to consider its effects on unrelated users and services,” the report reads.
Targeting the right layer is particularly important when it comes to VPNs. Consumer VPN services and corporate networks rely on many of the same underlying technologies, including protocols such as OpenVPN and WireGuard.
The report notes that Russia’s reported blocking of these VPN protocols shows how hard it is to tell the different uses apart at the network level.
When it comes to liability, i2Coalition points to the U.S. Supreme Court’s Cox ruling from earlier this year. This ruling confirmed that continuing to provide an Internet service, while knowing that some customers may misuse it, isn’t enough on its own to establish contributory copyright infringement.
The group sees the principles from this ruling as relevant to VPNs as well, but it doesn’t claim the matter is settled.
“If providers face liability merely because general-purpose services can be misused, they may have strong incentives to terminate users, restrict access, or intervene preemptively even when they have limited knowledge of the underlying conduct. Obligations should therefore reflect what an intermediary can reasonably know, control, and address,” the report warns.
“We see those principles as relevant to the debate around VPNs, but we aren’t suggesting that the ruling automatically determines the outcome of every VPN case. That would depend on the facts and legal issues presented,” Dawson notes.
VPN providers are not completely without responsibilities. According to the report, they can strengthen trust through independent audits and cooperation with legitimate legal processes. Voluntary programs, such as the VPN Trust Initiative’s own Trust Seal, can complement these efforts.
Lawmakers, in turn, should involve VPN providers and other technical experts from the start when they want to tackle a problem.
Silent on U.S. Bills
The report doesn’t apply these recommendations to the pending site blocking bills, as neither ACPA nor DEFEND IP is mentioned.
That’s notable, as ACPA would allow courts to name VPN providers with 100,000 or more monthly U.S. users or subscribers in a blocking order. That’s a position VPN companies would rather not be in.
TorrentFreak asked i2Coalition why the report doesn’t mention the two bills. Dawson says that the group is following both proposals, but that this particular report focuses on other developments.
“For this edition, we’ve focused on the developments covered in the report rather than trying to capture every pending legislative proposal. We expect to revisit US legislation in a future update as the debate develops,” Dawson says.
For now, both bills remain pending. Issa retires at the end of the year and Tillis’s term ends in January, so both bills would have to move ahead before the current session closes.
—
A copy of i2Coalition’s “VPNs at Risk” report is available here (pdf).
articles.summary:
The i2Coalition released a new report warning that forcing VPN providers to block pirate websites threatens neutral internet infrastructure and risks harming legitimate users and corporate networks.

### Key Points
- The "VPNs at Risk" report argues against using general-purpose internet infrastructure as a tool for copyright enforcement.
- French courts recently ordered major providers, including NordVPN and ExpressVPN, to block pirate sports streaming domains.
- Legal appeals regarding these blocking orders are currently pending before France’s Supreme Court, the Cour de cassation.
- The report highlights that VPNs share underlying technologies with corporate networks, making it difficult to restrict traffic without collateral damage.
- U.S. legislative proposals like the American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA) could mandate that VPNs with over 100,000 users implement site-blocking measures.

### Why it Matters
This debate highlights a growing tension between copyright enforcement efforts and the preservation of a neutral, open internet. If lawmakers successfully mandate blocking at the VPN level, it could set a precedent that forces infrastructure providers to monitor and restrict user traffic, potentially undermining privacy and security for all users.

articles.title: the hidden landscape of the digital world: what it takes to keep technology running
articles.author: thomai tsimpou I designboom
articles.content:
[FEATURED]
the ‘cloud’ is physical: the hidden infrastructure behind digital life
The digital world is often described as immaterial, a space of information that moves invisibly between devices and across networks. The term ‘cloud,’ for instance, suggests an ethereal space where data like photos, images and more can be stored without occupying any tangible place. In reality, though, these files reside on physical servers housed in data centers, supported by networks, cooling systems, and energy infrastructure. Every search, video stream, and artificial intelligence query depends on systems that consume energy, water, land, and raw materials. From mineral extraction and semiconductor manufacturing to data centers and electronic waste, the infrastructure behind digital life has a substantial environmental footprint.
As demand for computation increases, we need to reconsider how these systems are designed and what their growth requires from the planet and humanity. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centers consumed approximately 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025. The agency projects that this figure could approach 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, driven in part by the expansion of artificial intelligence and other computationally intensive services. These figures reveal the growing physical demands behind technologies that are often presented detached from material reality. They also raise a fundamental question: can the digital economy become more sustainable if the infrastructure supporting it continues to expand?
the material origins of computation
The environmental footprint of digital technology begins before a device is switched on. Smartphones, computers, servers, and networking equipment depend on minerals extracted, processed, and transported through global supply chains. Copper carries electricity and data through physical networks, while other metals and specialized materials are used in circuit boards, batteries, and semiconductor components. Their extraction can require substantial energy and water, while mining and processing can disrupt landscapes and generate pollution. Electrification, transport, and renewable energy systems depend on mineral-intensive supply chains. However, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure adds another source of demand, particularly as data centers require large quantities of servers and supporting equipment.
Semiconductor manufacturing introduces another layer of environmental complexity. Producing advanced chips involves highly controlled industrial environments, energy-intensive processes, and significant water requirements. A 2023 study examining environmental disclosures from 28 semiconductor companies reported approximately 789 million cubic meters of water withdrawals and 149 billion kilowatt-hours of energy consumption across the companies surveyed. These figures do not represent the entire global semiconductor industry, but they illustrate the scale of the resources involved in manufacturing the components that make modern computing possible.
data centers as physical architecture
Data centers house the servers that store and process the information we access every day. They require a lot of supporting infrastructure, from backup power systems to cooling equipment that prevents the machines from overheating. Where these facilities are built matters. Their location affects the availability of electricity and water, while the design of their cooling systems influences how much of each resource they consume. As more data centers are built to meet growing demand, their impact on local infrastructure becomes harder to ignore. Cooling is particularly important because computing equipment converts much of the electricity it uses into heat. That heat must be removed to maintain reliable operating conditions, creating an additional energy demand. Depending on the facility and its climate, cooling may rely on mechanical refrigeration, air-based systems, liquid cooling, or combinations of different technologies.
Even if a data center uses energy efficiently, it can still put pressure on the local electricity grid or consume water that is already in demand by nearby communities. The impact depends partly on where the facility is built and what resources are available there. A cooling system that works well in one location may be less suitable in another, particularly in areas where water is scarce. The location of a data center, its energy supply, and the way it is cooled are just as important as the technology inside it. These decisions are often made long before the servers start running, but they can determine how the facility affects its surroundings for years to come.
when efficiency is not enough
More efficient servers and cooling systems can reduce the energy needed to run a data center, but they do not necessarily reduce its total consumption. As computing capacity grows and new applications emerge, demand can rise faster than efficiency improves. This is particularly relevant to artificial intelligence, which requires computing power both to train models and to run them for users. As these services become more widely available, the amount of computation they require increases, even as the hardware becomes more efficient.
A data center may use less electricity to process each request but still consume more energy overall if it handles many more requests. The distinction matters when assessing the environmental impact of digital technology. Efficiency gains are useful, but they tell only part of the story. Total electricity consumption, water use, and demand on local infrastructure also need to be considered. The same applies to renewable energy. Using renewable electricity can reduce emissions associated with the power supply of a data center, but it does not address every part of its environmental footprint. The facility still requires land, construction materials, servers, and cooling systems, while the manufacture and eventual disposal of its equipment carry their own costs.
water, heat, and the possibilities of reuse
Water consumption is one of the most widely discussed environmental concerns surrounding data centers, particularly in regions already facing water shortages. Some facilities rely on water-based cooling to prevent servers from overheating, although consumption varies depending on the cooling system, climate, and operating conditions. Choosing where to build a data center is closely tied to the availability of local resources. Cooling systems also involve trade-offs. Air-based cooling, liquid cooling, and other approaches differ in their energy requirements, water consumption, and operating costs. No single solution works best in every setting, making local climate and resource availability important factors in the design of these facilities.
Heat is another part of the equation. Data centers generate large amounts of waste heat, which is usually removed from the building and released into the environment. In some cases, this heat can be recovered and used to warm nearby buildings or supply district heating networks, turning an operational by-product into a potential energy source. A 2024 study examined the potential for integrating data center waste heat into a district heating system in Italy. In the modeled scenarios, recovered heat supplied between 12 and 59 percent of the district heating mix, while gas consumption fell by approximately 11 to 58 percent. These figures represent modeled outcomes rather than measured savings from an operating facility, but they illustrate the potential benefits of connecting data centers to existing heating infrastructure. Unlike cooling, which is primarily concerned with managing the heat generated by servers, heat recovery looks at how that energy might be put to use. Its feasibility depends on factors such as the temperature of the recovered heat, the distance to potential users, and whether demand for heating coincides with its availability.
the problem of electronic waste
The environmental cost of digital technology continues after equipment leaves service. Servers, computers, phones, and networking hardware contain materials that can be recovered, but they also include components and substances that make safe processing difficult. When electronics are discarded without appropriate collection and treatment, valuable resources are lost and harmful materials can enter the environment. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reported that the world generated 62 billion kilograms of electronic waste in 2022. Only 22.3 percent of that total was documented as formally collected and recycled in an environmentally sound manner. The report projects that global e-waste could reach 82 billion kilograms by 2030.
Data centers regularly replace servers and other equipment to meet performance and reliability requirements. Newer hardware can process more information using less energy per task, but manufacturing it also requires new materials and energy. Whether replacing older equipment reduces the overall environmental impact depends on how much energy is saved during operation and what it takes to produce the replacement. Keeping equipment in use for longer can help reduce the need for new hardware. Servers that can be repaired, upgraded, and maintained are less likely to need replacing as soon as their performance begins to fall behind. When equipment reaches the end of its useful life, recycling can recover some of its materials for future use, although recycling alone does not address the resources required to manufacture new devices in the first place. Extending the life of working equipment, repairing components where possible, and recovering materials when equipment can no longer be used all have a role in reducing electronic waste.
designing for a less extractive digital future
Reducing the environmental impact of digital technology involves more than making servers faster or data centers more energy-efficient. It also means looking at where facilities are built, how they are cooled and powered, how long equipment remains in use, and what happens to it when it is replaced. Recovering waste heat, using renewable electricity, and designing equipment that can be repaired or reused can all help, but their benefits depend on how these measures are put into practice.
For architects and designers, data centers raise questions that go beyond the buildings themselves. Their energy and water needs affect the places where they operate, while their construction and equipment depend on materials sourced from elsewhere. Decisions about location, infrastructure, and maintenance can have consequences long after a facility is built. There is also the question of how much computing we actually need. As artificial intelligence and other digital services continue to expand, improving efficiency will not necessarily reduce overall resource use. The growing demand for computation deserves as much attention as the technologies developed to meet it. The cloud may feel distant from the physical world, but its infrastructure is not. It exists in mines, factories, warehouses, power stations, and data centers, all drawing on resources and leaving an environmental footprint. Recognizing this is a starting point for thinking differently about digital technology, not as something separate from the environment, but as part of it.

The digital "cloud" relies on extensive physical infrastructure, including data centers and semiconductor manufacturing, which consume significant energy, water, and raw materials while generating substantial electronic waste.

### Key Points
- The International Energy Agency projects data center electricity consumption could reach 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, up from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025.
- Semiconductor manufacturing is highly resource-intensive, with 28 surveyed companies reporting 789 million cubic meters of water withdrawals and 149 billion kilowatt-hours of energy use in 2023.
- Global electronic waste reached 62 billion kilograms in 2022, with only 22.3 percent formally recycled, a figure projected to rise to 82 billion kilograms by 2030.
- Data centers generate significant waste heat, which some experimental projects are attempting to repurpose for district heating to improve overall energy efficiency.
- Efficiency gains in hardware are often offset by the rapid growth in demand for computationally intensive services like artificial intelligence.

### Why it Matters
The rapid expansion of digital infrastructure creates a tangible environmental footprint that challenges the perception of the cloud as an immaterial space. Understanding these physical demands is essential for developing sustainable technology policies that account for resource scarcity and long-term ecological impact.

articles.title: Prolo Ring Lets You Click and Scroll Without a Mouse
articles.author: Ida Torres
articles.content:
There are days when you work on just your laptop. And then there are days when you have to switch between different devices and therefore also use different controllers. If you have a huge desk or workspace, then that’s probably fine. But if you’re working in a limited space, then the different controllers add to the clutter. What if you have something that can fit onto a finger and let you switch between different devices more easily?
That’s the promise that the Wearable Ring Controller by Prolo is making. Called the Prolo Ring, it is a Bluetooth wearable input controller that can be worn on your index finger. It has a trackpad that your thumb can use to move the cursor and scroll, and a touch strip that your other hand’s index finger can operate. The Pro Edition even supports air gestures, giving you another way to control your devices.
Designer: Prolo
The most noticeable design choice is its wide band. This gives your thumb room to work with an 18 × 30 mm capacitive touch surface rather than a tiny button. According to Prolo, the ring measures 23 mm wide and 2.9 mm thick and weighs between 4.1 and 5.2 grams. Its shell is made from polycarbonate, despite the metallic-looking finishes available for the Pro Edition. The broad profile makes it look more like a wearable tool than a discreet piece of jewelry.
That width also makes sizing important. Prolo lists US sizes 7–18 and requires test wear with its sizing kit or a 3D-printed sizer before you confirm your size. Your usual jewelry size may not translate directly to this wider band. Included adjustment shims help fine-tune a slightly loose fit. You can wear it on either index finger, keeping the trackpad facing your thumb.
The top touch strip, called the Modstrip, handles mode switching and additional commands. The four modes are Cursor, Navigation, Touch, and Air, organizing functions such as pointing, browsing, media playback, and motion gestures. Separating these controls lets the same small surface perform different jobs, although it also means learning which mode you’re using. Some interactions require both hands.
One particularly interesting feature is Joystick Assist. Swipe quickly from one edge of the trackpad to the other and keep holding, and the cursor continues moving. Moving your thumb farther from the center increases its speed; releasing stops it. This addresses the limited travel of a finger-sized trackpad, while ordinary trackpad movements remain available for finer positioning.
Switching devices uses a tap followed by a hold on the Modstrip. The ring disconnects from the current device and reconnects to another saved device, so “instantly” would be an overstatement. It connects to only one device at a time. For someone moving between a laptop and a tablet, the appeal is keeping the same controller rather than reaching for another one.
Basic controls use standard Bluetooth HID, the protocol used by compatible input devices, without requiring a dedicated driver or app. Prolo lists support for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS/iPadOS, plus compatible smart TVs and XR devices. Available functions vary by device and app. It can also work alongside your existing mouse and keyboard rather than requiring you to replace them.
The Pro Edition adds more than 40 customizable gestures, assignable shortcuts, macros, and profiles. Prolo Studio, the free desktop companion app, handles customization. You could organize controls around presentations or media playback rather than use every available gesture. Push-to-talk can trigger dictation or AI shortcuts, but the ring has no microphone; a connected device handles the voice input.
Prolo claims up to 10 hours of typical use per charge and includes a magnetic charging cable. The ring is not waterproof, so it needs to come off before showering or swimming. For cramped workspaces, its clearest potential benefit is freeing you from needing a separate mousing surface. Whether that convenience outweighs wearing a broad band and learning its controls will depend on how you work.

- The Pro Edition supports over 40 customizable air gestures, macros, and shortcuts via the Prolo Studio desktop application.

### Why it Matters
This wearable technology offers a space-saving alternative for professionals managing multiple devices in cramped workspaces by eliminating the need for a dedicated mouse surface. By consolidating input controls into a single finger-worn device, it provides a versatile, cross-platform solution for users who frequently switch between laptops, tablets, and smart TVs.
